summary: In 2006 the IETF published SPF and Sender ID as two experimental email authentication protocols. This informational RFC reports on the resolution of those experiments and how the concerns about their conflicts were addressed.

plainLanguage.summary: Two similar mail-checking systems were tried to see which worked better. This memo explains what was decided after the test.

questions: what happened to the sender id experiment
how was the spf experiment resolved
why did the spf dns record type 99 fail
what is the submitter smtp extension
subtitle: A report card on SPF and Sender ID: after six years of surveys, SPF won and the experiments were declared concluded.

tldr.problem: In 2006 the IESG published SPF and Sender ID as Experimental because the two email authentication protocols could conflict operationally, and it asked the community to observe them for two years.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC collects DNS surveys, implementation counts, SUBMITTER extension surveys and result comparisons gathered over six years, and draws conclusions from that evidence.
tldr.outcome: The experiments are concluded. SPF had widespread implementation and deployment, while the SPF DNS record type (99), Sender ID, PRA and SUBMITTER saw little adoption.

today: RFC 6686 is an Informational RFC (July 2012), and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It records the end of the SPF and Sender ID experiments rather than defining a protocol.

sections.title: Two Experiments and a Verdict
sections.content:
In April 2006 the IETF published SPF and Sender ID, two email authentication protocols. Sender ID consists of three documents. Both let a domain publish, through the DNS, a policy saying which mail servers may send email for that domain name.

Consensus did not clearly favor either one, and there was concern that they would conflict in some operational situations and interfere with delivery. The IESG therefore required all the documents (RFC 4405, RFC 4406, RFC 4407 and RFC 4408) to be published as Experimental and asked the community to watch deployment for two years.

This RFC, written after six years, concludes the experiments. It makes no technical comparison of correctness or weaknesses. It only reports what was deployed and supported.
sections.plainLanguage: Two clubs both wanted to be the official way to check that mail is really from who it says. Grown-ups let both try for a while, then looked at which one people actually used.

sections.title: SPF Records in the DNS
sections.content:
SPF policies can be published in two RRTYPEs (DNS resource record types): TXT (16) and the dedicated SPF type (99). Three large DNS surveys looked for both. Records counted only if they began with v=spf1 or spf2.0/.

In every survey, TXT replies far outnumbered SPF-type replies. Survey #1 (Cisco) queried 1,000,000 domains and saw 397,511 TXT replies against 6,627 SPF replies. Survey #2 (The Trusted Domain Project) queried 278,353 and saw 156,894 against 2,876. Survey #3 (Hotmail) queried 100,000 and saw 46,221 against 954.

In survey #2, 4,360 domains (over 1.6%) answered the TXT query in time N while the SPF-type query ultimately failed after at least time 4N. A separate look at nameserver traffic found only a few queries for type 99, almost all from one large email provider.
sections.plainLanguage: Most people wrote their mail rules on the old noticeboard everyone already checked, and almost nobody used the new noticeboard.

sections.title: Implementations and SUBMITTER
sections.content:
Which servers check SPF or Sender ID cannot be learned by a survey, so the authors used web searches. A Sender ID site last updated in late 2007 listed 13 commercial implementations and no free open-source ones. The OpenSPF site listed six libraries, 22 mail transfer agents with built-in SPF, and many patches, a mix of commercial and open source.

The SUBMITTER SMTP extension gives the receiving server an early hint of the Purported Responsible Address (PRA), which Sender ID uses. Of 484,980 MTAs selected, 371,779 responded, and 17,425 (4.7%) had SUBMITTER enabled. Of those advertising it, 97% were instances of a single MTA.

Comparing results, Trusted Domain Project data on about 150,000 messages showed Sender ID and SPF reaching the same conclusion more than 95% of the time. Hotmail's analysis over billions of messages found about 80%. Differences have not been noted as causing significant operational problems.
sections.plainLanguage: Many tools knew how to use the first system, far fewer knew the second, and when both were asked about the same letter they usually agreed.

sections.title: Analysis and Conclusions
sections.content:
The analysis found no substantial adoption of RRTYPE 99: fewer than 2% of responding domains published it and almost no clients asked for it. Fewer than 3% of records requested PRA processing, an essential part of Sender ID. No data showed a substantial accuracy benefit to either approach, and SPF implementations showed better upkeep. Obstacles to new RRTYPEs included firewalls and DNS servers that block unknown types, and DNS tools that lack support.

The conclusions are that the four experiments (SUBMITTER, Sender ID, PRA and SPF) should be considered concluded; RRTYPE 99 has not attracted enough support to be useful; and Sender ID, PRA and SUBMITTER lack a strong community. Finally, SPF has widespread implementation and deployment, comparable to that of many Standards Track protocols.
sections.plainLanguage: Almost everyone picked the first club. So the trial is over, the first club is the winner, and the second club's special noticeboard did not catch on.

sections.title: Why the New Record Type Failed
sections.content:
Appendix A explains the RRTYPE problem. SPF began outside the IETF, and by the time it arrived there a large installed base already used TXT records. A new type was applied for under pressure from DNS experts and assigned long after the IESG approved SPF. A plan to transition gradually to type 99 failed for four reasons: existing nameservers and DNS-aware firewalls dropped unknown types, DNS provisioning tools were slow to add support, TXT was already working, and the SPF specification said a domain SHOULD publish both types and MUST publish at least one, so two compliant parties could fail to interoperate.

The author warns this is likely to recur unless the bar to create new RRTYPEs is lowered and software handles unknown types gracefully. He notes the requirements had since become less stringent (RFC 6195) and that RFC 5507 offers guidance.
sections.plainLanguage: The new noticeboard was installed late, some doors would not even open for it, and everyone was happy with the old one, so nobody moved.
